problems.title: Parking Lot
problems.description: Design a parking lot system that tracks available spots across multiple vehicle types, calculates a parking fee on exit, and handles a full lot.
requirements: Park a vehicle in an available spot and unpark it later
Support at least two vehicle/spot types (e.g. compact and large)
Calculate a fee based on how long the vehicle was parked
Reject parking when the lot is full, rather than crashing or silently failing

problems.title: Vending Machine
problems.description: Design a vending machine that accepts payment, dispenses a selected item, and handles out-of-stock items and insufficient payment.
requirements: Select an item and dispense it if in stock and paid for
Accept at least two payment methods
Handle an out-of-stock selection without crashing
Return change (or reject the transaction) on incorrect payment

problems.title: Elevator System
problems.description: Design an elevator control system for a building with multiple elevators, handling floor call requests and dispatching the most appropriate elevator.
requirements: Request an elevator from a floor (up or down)
Select a destination floor from inside a car
Dispatch a reasonable elevator among multiple available ones
Handle more than one simultaneous request without contradicting itself

criteria.name: Requirement Coverage
criteria.description: Does the design actually address the stated requirements, including the less obvious ones (concurrency of access, capacity limits, pricing variation)?

scoringGuidance.excellent: Every stated requirement maps to a clear place in the design, including edge cases like a full lot or an unpaid exit.
scoringGuidance.good: Core requirements are covered; one or two secondary requirements are thin or implicit.
scoringGuidance.weak: Only the obvious happy-path requirement (park a car) is addressed.
scoringGuidance.poor: The design doesn't clearly address the problem's stated requirements at all.

criteria.name: Domain Modeling
criteria.description: Are the entities, value objects, and relationships the right shape for this problem — not too many, not too few?

scoringGuidance.excellent: Entities map cleanly to real concepts in the problem; relationships and cardinality are explicit and correct.
scoringGuidance.good: Reasonable entities with a couple of debatable choices (e.g. a missing value object, an over-broad class).
scoringGuidance.weak: Entities exist but blur multiple concepts together, or invent structure the problem doesn't need.
scoringGuidance.poor: No real modeling — a bag of fields and functions with no entity boundaries.

criteria.name: Encapsulation & Responsibilities
criteria.description: Does each class own a clear, singular responsibility, with internal state protected behind behavior rather than exposed as public fields?

scoringGuidance.excellent: Each class has one clear reason to change; internal state is private and mutated only through methods that preserve invariants.
scoringGuidance.good: Mostly clean, with one class doing slightly more than it should.
scoringGuidance.weak: Multiple unrelated responsibilities are concentrated in one or two classes.
scoringGuidance.poor: State is public and mutated from anywhere; no real encapsulation.

criteria.name: Extensibility
criteria.description: If a likely requirement changes (new pricing rule, new vehicle type, new payment method), how much existing code has to change?

scoringGuidance.excellent: Likely requirement changes need minimal modification to existing classes — new behavior slots in behind an existing seam.
scoringGuidance.good: Some extension points exist, but certain changes would still touch existing responsibilities.
scoringGuidance.weak: Significant conditional logic (long if/switch chains) or tight coupling would need untangling.
scoringGuidance.poor: The design is highly coupled and difficult to extend without a rewrite.

criteria.name: SOLID / Design Quality
criteria.description: Where SOLID principles or a design pattern would genuinely help, are they applied — and not applied where they wouldn't?

scoringGuidance.excellent: SOLID principles are visibly respected where it matters; any pattern used earns its place rather than being decorative.
scoringGuidance.good: Generally sound, with one principle bent for a reason that's at least defensible.
scoringGuidance.weak: Clear violations (e.g. a class that both decides and executes, or subclassing used for what should be composition).
scoringGuidance.poor: No apparent awareness of responsibility separation.

criteria.name: Trade-offs & Explanation
criteria.description: Does the submission explain *why* it made its key decisions, including what it chose not to do and why?

scoringGuidance.excellent: Key decisions are explained with real trade-offs named (what was gained, what was given up, what would change under different constraints).
scoringGuidance.good: Some rationale given, but mostly assertion rather than trade-off reasoning.
scoringGuidance.weak: Little to no explanation of why the design looks the way it does.

criteria.evidence: parkVehicle() and unparkVehicle() handle the core flow and calculateFee() computes a fee, but there's no handling for a full lot or multiple vehicle types.
criteria.feedback: Core parking/unparking and fee calculation are present; the full-lot and multi-vehicle-type requirements aren't addressed.
criteria.suggestion: Add an explicit check and response for when no spots are available.

criteria.evidence: ParkingLot is the only class; the ideas of a spot, a vehicle, and a payment are implied by method names but never given their own type.
criteria.feedback: The single class captures the workflow but doesn't model the underlying concepts separately.
criteria.suggestion: Introduce Spot and Vehicle as explicit types.

criteria.evidence: processPayment() and generateReceipt() are both methods directly on ParkingLot, alongside the parking logic itself.
criteria.feedback: Payment and receipt behavior are handled inline rather than owned by a collaborator whose job they actually are.
criteria.suggestion: Extract payment and receipt generation into their own classes.

criteria.evidence: calculateFee() is a method on ParkingLot itself with a hardcoded flat rate, so a new pricing rule means editing ParkingLot directly.
criteria.feedback: Pricing changes require modifying ParkingLot — there's no seam for a new pricing rule.
criteria.suggestion: Extract pricing behind a PricingStrategy interface so a new rule is a new class, not an edit to ParkingLot.

criteria.evidence: ParkingLot has five responsibilities: parking, unparking, fee calculation, payment processing, and receipt generation.
criteria.feedback: This concentrates responsibilities that could each change for independent reasons — a Single Responsibility concern.
criteria.suggestion: Split payment processing and receipt generation into their own collaborators.

criteria.evidence: The submission has no accompanying explanation of why it's structured this way.
criteria.feedback: No trade-offs or rationale are given for the design's current shape.
criteria.suggestion: Add a short note on what was prioritized and what was deliberately left out.

weaknesses: Encapsulation & Responsibilities: Payment and receipt behavior are handled inline rather than owned by a collaborator whose job they actually are.
Extensibility: Pricing changes require modifying ParkingLot — there's no seam for a new pricing rule.
Trade-offs & Explanation: No trade-offs or rationale are given for the design's current shape.
suggestions: Extract payment and receipt generation into their own classes.
Extract pricing behind a PricingStrategy interface so a new rule is a new class, not an edit to ParkingLot.
Add a short note on what was prioritized and what was deliberately left out.

criteria.evidence: SpotManager.findAvailableSpot() explicitly returns null when the lot is full, which parkVehicle() checks before proceeding.
criteria.feedback: Core flow plus the full-lot edge case are now handled explicitly rather than assumed away.
criteria.suggestion: Consider also handling a vehicle attempting to unpark twice.

criteria.evidence: SpotManager, PricingStrategy, PaymentProcessor, and ReceiptService are now separate types alongside ParkingLot.
criteria.feedback: The concepts underlying the workflow now have their own representation instead of being implicit in method names.
criteria.suggestion: A Vehicle type (rather than a raw license plate string) would complete the picture.

criteria.evidence: ParkingLot now delegates to spotManager, pricingStrategy, and paymentProcessor rather than doing the work itself.
criteria.feedback: Responsibilities are owned by the collaborator whose job they actually are.
criteria.suggestion: No changes needed for this MVP scope.

criteria.evidence: PricingStrategy is an interface with HourlyPricing as one implementation, injected into ParkingLot's constructor.
criteria.feedback: A new pricing rule is now a new class implementing PricingStrategy, not an edit to ParkingLot.
criteria.suggestion: The same seam could be extended to PaymentProcessor for multiple payment methods.

criteria.evidence: Payment processing and receipt generation were extracted into PaymentProcessor and ReceiptService, leaving ParkingLot to coordinate spot allocation.
criteria.feedback: ParkingLot's remaining responsibility is much closer to a single reason to change.
criteria.suggestion: No changes needed for this MVP scope.

criteria.evidence: A comment on the submission states PricingStrategy was introduced specifically so pricing changes don't touch ParkingLot, and that multi-currency was left out of scope.
criteria.feedback: One clear trade-off is named, with an explicit statement of what was deliberately deferred.
criteria.suggestion: Naming a second trade-off (e.g. why SpotManager doesn't reserve spot types) would strengthen this further.

strengths: Requirement Coverage: Core flow plus the full-lot edge case are now handled explicitly rather than assumed away.
Domain Modeling: The concepts underlying the workflow now have their own representation instead of being implicit in method names.
Encapsulation & Responsibilities: Responsibilities are owned by the collaborator whose job they actually are.
Extensibility: A new pricing rule is now a new class implementing PricingStrategy, not an edit to ParkingLot.
SOLID / Design Quality: ParkingLot's remaining responsibility is much closer to a single reason to change.

criteria.evidence: The design includes selectItem, makePayment with CashPayment, CardPayment and UPIPayment, out‑of‑stock handling ("Item is out of stock"), and change return for cash payments.
criteria.feedback: Core functional requirements are implemented and demonstrated in the example usage. Edge cases such as concurrency, inventory capacity limits, and dynamic pricing are not addressed.
criteria.suggestion: Add thread‑safe handling for concurrent selections and a way to configure stock limits or price rules to cover the less obvious requirements.

criteria.evidence: Entities like Item, ItemSlot, Inventory, PaymentMethod (interface) and VendingMachineState are defined, each reflecting a real concept of the problem.
criteria.feedback: The model captures the main concepts without unnecessary complexity. A dedicated Money/value‑object could improve type safety for prices and amounts.
criteria.suggestion: Introduce a Money value object to encapsulate currency arithmetic and avoid raw number usage for prices and payments.

criteria.evidence: Fields such as quantity, slots and state are private; public behavior (dispense, addItem, makePayment) manipulates them. SelectedItem is public but only mutated through VendingMachine methods.
criteria.feedback: Encapsulation is generally good, but exposing selectedItem as a public field and providing getQuantity may leak internal state.
criteria.suggestion: Make selectedItem private and expose read‑only accessors; consider removing getQuantity or returning a read‑only view.

criteria.evidence: The comment "Easy to add later without modifying VendingMachine" and the Strategy pattern for PaymentMethod illustrate extension points; new states can be added via the State pattern.
criteria.feedback: Adding new payment methods or states is straightforward, but some coupling remains (VendingMachine directly calls inventory.dispense and processes payment).
criteria.suggestion: Introduce interfaces for dispensing and transaction handling so VendingMachine depends on abstractions, reducing the need to modify it for future changes.

criteria.evidence: Single Responsibility is claimed: Inventory manages stock, PaymentMethod manages payment, VendingMachine coordinates, States control valid operations. Open/Closed is used for payments.
criteria.feedback: VendingMachine.processPayment mixes payment validation and dispensing, violating SRP. Also, state methods signatures are inconsistent (makePayment missing parameters in IdleState).
criteria.suggestion: Extract dispensing logic into a separate service and ensure all state classes strictly follow the VendingMachineState interface signature.

criteria.evidence: The "DESIGN TRADE-OFFS" section explains why State and Strategy patterns were chosen, their benefits and limitations, and mentions failure handling and extensibility considerations.
criteria.feedback: The trade‑off discussion is clear and ties decisions to concrete benefits and potential drawbacks.
criteria.suggestion: Include a brief note on the runtime overhead of the State pattern and how it was deemed acceptable for this domain.

strengths: Domain Modeling: The model captures the main concepts without unnecessary complexity. A dedicated Money/value‑object could improve type safety for prices and amounts.
Encapsulation & Responsibilities: Encapsulation is generally good, but exposing selectedItem as a public field and providing getQuantity may leak internal state.
Extensibility: Adding new payment methods or states is straightforward, but some coupling remains (VendingMachine directly calls inventory.dispense and processes payment).
Trade-offs & Explanation: The trade‑off discussion is clear and ties decisions to concrete benefits and potential drawbacks.

criteria.evidence: findAvailableSpot returns null // lot is full — handled explicitly, and parkVehicle/unparkVehicle implement entry, exit and fee calculation
criteria.feedback: The design meets core requirements (parking, unparking, fee calculation, full‑lot handling) but does not model multiple vehicle/spot types or address concurrency, which are part of the stated requirements.
criteria.suggestion: Add Spot types (e.g., compact, large) and a Vehicle type hierarchy, and consider thread‑safe access to shared state.

criteria.evidence: SpotManager uses a Map<string, boolean> for spots and ParkingLot stores licensePlate strings in a Map; there is no explicit Spot or Vehicle entity.
criteria.feedback: The model captures the essential behavior but conflates concepts (spot is just an id/boolean, vehicle is just a string), missing natural domain objects and their attributes.
criteria.suggestion: Introduce Spot and Vehicle/value‑object classes with properties such as spotId, spotType, licensePlate, vehicleType to make the domain clearer.

criteria.evidence: private spots = new Map<string, boolean>(); with occupy/release methods, and private occupiedBy map inside ParkingLot; state is never exposed publicly.
criteria.feedback: State is well‑encapsulated and mutated only through dedicated methods, preserving invariants.
criteria.suggestion: Consider adding validation inside SpotManager methods (e.g., prevent occupying an already occupied spot) to tighten invariants.

criteria.evidence: PricingStrategy interface allows new pricing rules, but vehicle/spot types are hard‑coded and ParkingLot depends on concrete SpotManager, PaymentProcessor, ReceiptService.
criteria.feedback: Pricing is extensible, yet adding new vehicle or spot types would require changes in multiple classes, limiting overall extensibility.
criteria.suggestion: Introduce abstractions for SpotManager (e.g., ISpotRepository) and for vehicle handling, and make spot selection strategy pluggable.

criteria.evidence: Separate classes for pricing, payment, receipt, spot management; each has a single responsibility. PricingStrategy follows OCP. ParkingLot directly uses concrete collaborators.
criteria.feedback: Good adherence to SRP and OCP for pricing; however, Dependency Inversion is only partially applied because ParkingLot depends on concrete implementations rather than interfaces.
criteria.suggestion: Define interfaces for payment processing and receipt issuance and have ParkingLot depend on those abstractions.

criteria.evidence: Comment: "PricingStrategy was introduced specifically so a new pricing rule ... is a new class, not an edit to ParkingLot. Multi-currency support was deliberately left out of scope."
criteria.feedback: The submission explains the main trade‑off (pricing extensibility vs. scope) but provides limited discussion of other decisions such as spot modeling or concurrency.
criteria.suggestion: Expand the trade‑off section to cover why spot types were omitted, why concurrency was not addressed, and what would change if those concerns were added.

strengths: Encapsulation & Responsibilities: State is well‑encapsulated and mutated only through dedicated methods, preserving invariants.

SOLID / Design Quality: Good adherence to SRP and OCP for pricing; however, Dependency Inversion is only partially applied because ParkingLot depends on concrete implementations rather than interfaces.
